extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, judges, forensic psychologists, legal investigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing confessions, partial admissions, witness testimony, and causal reconstruction in criminal investigations; emphasizes psychological context, motive analysis, and rigorous chaining of causes. Intended to direct legal/forensic practitioners in assessing probative value and avoiding common reasoning errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceive confessions in full psychological and contextual terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a confession is insufficient; we must understand the confession in terms of all the factors that caused it. A confession is only established in truth when it is construed psychologically, when the whole inner life of the confessor and his external conditions are brought into relation with it, and the remaining motives established as at least possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating a confession as self-contained proof; investigate the confessor's capacities, passions, intentions, purposes, and external circumstances. Beware of the aphorism “what is reasserted is half proved,” and do not accept a confession at face value without motive analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apagogic (proof by negation) to discover motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of discovering the factors that caused a confession is purely logical and generally established indirectly by means of an apagogue (proof by negation): bring together all conceivable motives and study the confession with regard to them; if all or most are shown impossible or insufficient, the remaining conclusion(s) remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate possible motives, eliminate implausible ones, and treat the remaining explanations as the basis for psychological judgment. This method helps avoid premature acceptance of facile explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat partial confessions as especially problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial confessions make it harder to prove what is not confessed and can cast doubt on what is confessed; mistakes are possible even where confession and silence appear straightforward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze why only certain facts are admitted; consider incentives, hopes for gain, strategic self-protection, or attempts to assume others' guilt. Partial admissions require careful corroboration and motive analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the defendant’s legal knowledge when evaluating denials
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person who may be supposed to know the legal situation denies an element (e.g., intent to kill), this creates sufficient justification for doubting the honesty of his confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the defendant's sophistication and prior experience; deliberate denials by legally aware individuals may be strategic and warrant scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic inference from number of confessed acts to unconfessed acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition 'who has stolen one thing has also stolen the rest' has only slight justification; jurists may reasonably infer either way (that unconfessed items were taken or would have been confessed), but both inferences are not decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the sheer quantity of confessed items substitute for evidence on specific unconfessed items; consider significance for current and future proceedings (stigma, pattern evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for long-term consequences of conviction or confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a man pleads guilty or not guilty is never indifferent, since prior convictions or confessions can create lasting stigma and influence suspicion in later similar cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that past adjudications (or convictions based on confessions) may bias future investigations; preserve caution when relating prior findings to new suspicions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of victim-reported quantities and possible exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims of theft often count everything missing, may attribute pre-existing losses to the theft, or exaggerate quantities to excite sympathy or invoke help; servants or others may shift blame onto 'the thief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborate inventories and reported losses; treat inflated claims with caution and investigate alternative explanations for missing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume a confessor has little motive to deny facts that cause no added harm
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no psychological reason that a confessor should deny anything the confession of which can bring him no additional harm; the accused's viewpoint must be studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an accused denies matters that would not materially increase punishment, consider psychological explanations (obstinacy, pride, perverted viewpoint) rather than automatic presumption of innocence or guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate the 'pure kernel' when a confessor implicates a fellow-criminal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a denying fellow-criminal is accused by a confession, the pure kernel of the confession must be brought to light and everything that might free the confessor and involve the other set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the situation twice—once without reference to the fellow and once with; eliminate additions motivated by self-preservation or malicious intent. This often requires complete control of material and is psychologically difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate motives for accusing accomplices
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusers may implicate companions out of revenge, hatred, jealousy, envy, anger, suspicion, business jealousy, or attempts to prevent disloyalty; such motives are often concealed and not easy to discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider interpersonal relations, opportunities for revenge or gain, and personality traits; use corroboration and psychological insight to assess whether implication of another is truthful or strategic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating side issues with the central issue of the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances denied that have no essential relation to the crime can divert presentation of proof so that the essential problem is neglected; proving such side issues is preparatory and must be cautiously weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat proof of peripheral facts (e.g., acquaintance with the victim) as conclusive proof of murder. Use examples (arsenic-poisoning case, mason accused of murder) to illustrate how proving side facts can mislead a case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the accused’s attitude/point-of-view in psychological analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused’s information and viewpoint must be studied; his motives, however perverted, often contain the key to understanding denials or confessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to understand advantages the accused seeks (e.g., avoiding public shame, preserving relationships) and how these shape statements; this perspective prevents misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware identification of inferred with perceived facts (witness suggestibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses and observers often conflate inference with perception; proving a side issue may cause them to believe the principal issue, and the mere appearance of arrest can convince many of guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against suggestibility, contextual bias (presentation of defendant in custody/stripes), and psychological conflation; corroborate identifications with independent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground case presentation in causal analysis (find efficient, satisfying causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminalist’s task is the study of causes: to find the causal chain of which the last link is the crime and to include only those events that are exclusively bound up with the accused’s criminality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically observe and correlate every detail, seeking causes for each element of the crime and integrating them into a coherent causal chain that shows the crime as the result of the accused's activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study causal conditions before searching for personality explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest mistakes occur when one seeks the personality of the criminal immediately instead of first studying the causal conditions of the crime; proper work uses the principle of causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reconstruction of events and causes; do not substitute speculative psychological profiling for demonstrable causal links between acts and the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish guilt by demonstrating the crime as the inevitable result of the accused’s activity alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of guilt is established only when the crime is accurately and explicitly described as the inevitable result of the activity of the criminal and his activity only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate every supposed action of the accused with the crime; demonstrate inevitability (to the extent possible) rather than mere possibility or association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of causal inference without prior experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the help of previous experience no causal nexus can be referred to an observation; a cause is a complex whose elements require reflection and enumeration to determine whether observations are singular or repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully enumerate observations and test whether they are genuine repeats or illusory; avoid over-generalizing from isolated instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to false causal correlations and similarity-based superstitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A common source of error is the supposition that cause must resemble effect (sympathetic magic, superstitions, or spurious analogies), which leads to false causal attributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and challenge subconscious similarity-based reasoning (e.g., patron-saint analogies, birth-night correlations); correct such correlations through explicit causal testing and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt suspect’s mental habits to correctly coordinate cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The most difficult part of causal coördination is adopting the point of view and mental habits of the person suspected of the effects; without this the causal relations arrived at by others may not be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruct the suspect’s perceptions, priorities, and patterns of association to see which causal links the suspect would have formed; this prevents misattribution of motives or causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine intermediary (proximate) links; do not accept omitted inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Many witnesses and lay people omit proximate causes as self-evident; failure to examine intermediary links can hide the source of error and produce extravagant, unjustified inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogate witnesses' chains of inference, identify omitted intermediaries (e.g., gravity vs. being thrown into water), and require justification for each causal step rather than accepting leaps.
